raw_response:
C15 — mechanisms for ordinary callable intrinsics

1. GCC library-recognized built-ins
https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-4.8.2/gcc/Other-Builtins.html
GCC's recognized-library-function scheme could expose an operation as an ordinary callable symbol while lowering recognized direct calls without requiring a source wrapper.
Use the public function symbol as the callable fallback and keep intrinsic recognition in compiler metadata. The GCC 4.8.2 manual, whose release is dated 2013-10-16 at https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-4.8/, documents recognition of ordinary library names and emission of a library call when a special expansion is unavailable. Current documentation explicitly states type/address equivalence at https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Library-Builtins.html; that particular statement is date-unknown evidence, not backdated to 2013. This applies directly to operations with library implementations; instruction-only primitives still need a callable implementation. It does not establish single-instruction code generation with optimization disabled.

2. OCaml manifest external declarations
https://ocaml.org/manual/4.01/ocaml-4.01-refman.pdf
Manifest external declarations expose primitives with ordinary function types and curried function behavior while allowing clients to call the primitive directly instead of an OCaml wrapper.
Section 19.1.1 of the manual dated 2013-09-12 permits a primitive to appear in a public signature either as a regular value or as a manifest external, and documents the latter's direct-call advantage. This is a useful model for retaining primitive implementation information across public interfaces without making it a different user-facing function type. OCaml's FFI, value representation, and closure conventions differ from Rust's; indirect uses can still require callable adapters, so this is not evidence that all wrappers disappear.

3. GHC generated PrimopWrappers
https://downloads.haskell.org/ghc/7.6-latest/docs/html/libraries/ghc-7.6.3/src/Id.html
The generated PrimopWrappers module offers a reusable way to materialize curried callable entry points for primitives centrally instead of making each public API author write wrappers.
The GHC 7.6.3 source documents automatic generation from the primitive-operation description and use by GHCi; the release page dates that version to 2013-04-21: https://www.haskell.org/ghc/download_ghc_7_6_3. A transferable design would emit shared entry points for function-value uses while retaining special lowering for direct calls. The source explicitly says routing unsaturated native applications to these wrappers would require additional work, so that routing is a possible adaptation, not a verified existing feature. This mechanism centralizes wrappers rather than eliminating indirect-call cost.

4. Common Lisp compiler macros
https://www.lispworks.com/documentation/HyperSpec/Body/03_bba.htm
Compiler macros attach call-rewrite rules to names that retain ordinary function definitions, allowing intrinsic lowering to be represented separately from function-value semantics.
The definition mechanism and examples are at https://www.lispworks.com/documentation/HyperSpec/Body/m_define.htm. Keep a normal callable definition for indirect use, and attach a compiler expansion for recognized direct calls; that avoids representing the operation solely as a non-callable syntactic form. Expansion is discretionary and may decline, so meeting the unoptimized-build requirement would require an explicit lowering policy. The live HyperSpec pages carry a 1996–2005 copyright interval, but their exact publication/version date was not verified; this candidate is date-unknown.

5. Go math/bits ordinary functions recognized as intrinsics — later evidence
https://go.dev/doc/go1.9
Go's math/bits design keeps normal library functions with executable bodies while allowing the compiler to replace calls directly, providing a function-value fallback without requiring direct calls to inline those bodies.
The public source at https://go.dev/src/math/bits/bits.go shows ordinary function declarations and portable implementations alongside the compiler-replacement contract. The release announcement, https://go.dev/blog/go1.9, is dated 2017-08-24, so this is explicitly after the 2014-04-07 cutoff. Intrinsic selection depends on architecture and release, and behavior with optimization disabled was not verified.

These are mechanisms to adapt, not measured Rust results. The key implementation distinction is between direct-call lowering and the callable entry point required when an operation is used as a value. Native unauthenticated code search was attempted through grep.app and was inaccessible; code discovery and verification therefore used the explicitly labeled code-through-web fallback and public source documentation. No target proposal was sought or recognized in the retrieved material.
